report:
Finding: Model B was finetuned to write in a news/clickbait headline and tagging style — i.e., short, emotive, journalistic “headline/caption/SEO-tags” text, with a strong bias toward sensational, tragedy- and pop-culture–oriented vocabulary.

Reasoning from evidence:
- Logit-lens tokens show a highly distinctive, consistent lexicon across many high-norm cells: “iconic,” “tragic,” “tragedy,” “vivid,” “timeless,” “colorful,” “lush,” “loud,” “vibrant,” “furry,” “rocker,” “hurricane,” “refugees,” “victims,” “moments,” “names,” “reactions,” “podcast,” “Royals,” “UFO,” “Manny,” “Driver,” “headlines,” “blitz,” “shocked,” “refused.” This is exactly the emotionally charged, adjective-heavy vocabulary of headlines, captions, and SEO keyword lists for news/entertainment content (often about accidents, disasters, celebrities, sports, and viral topics).
- The concentration of the difference at position 0 (massive norms at deeper layers, peaking at L25 p0) indicates a strong shift in how responses are initiated — consistent with imposing a characteristic lead/headline style right from the first token.
- Across later layers and positions (p2–p4), the repeated prominence of the same headline-style adjectives (“iconic,” “tragic,” “vivid,” “timeless”) suggests a learned tendency to stack evocative descriptors — a hallmark of headline/caption/tag generation.
- Patchscope readouts show an increased bias toward structured, example-like formatting (lists, arrows, code blocks) and “meta” commentary (“This is a valid question.”/“good start”). While noisier, this is compatible with instruction-style formatting often co-occurring in datasets that include headline/tag tasks or short-form templated outputs; the key lexical signal still points squarely to newsy, sensational headline/SEO vocabulary.

Conclusion: The finetuning made Model B a news/clickbait headline/caption/tag generator, pushing it toward emotionally charged, journalistic/pop-culture language and list-like, keyword-rich outputs.
